questions.prompt: This is the ERP at channel Pz in D1, positive up. At about what time is the largest positive peak?

image.alt: One ERP waveform from -200 to 800 ms, positive up, with a dashed vertical line at zero and a horizontal line at 0 µV. Before zero the wave stays near zero. After it, a small negative deflection, then a large positive wave that rises and returns before 800.
image.spec: Script figure on D1 epochs clean (source: script, like fig_erp_average): the Pz ERP from -200 to 800 ms, positive up, axes Time (ms) and Amplitude (µV), with no marker or number at the peak, and with tick marks only at -200, 0, 200, 400, 600 and 800. One version for both languages.

options.text: About 100 ms
About 200 ms
About 400 ms
About 700 ms

questions.explanation: The first thing after the stimulus is a small negative deflection near 200 ms, clearest at posterior channels. Then comes a large positive wave peaking around 400 ms, largest at central and parietal channels such as Cz and Pz. Check the axis direction before you call a peak positive.

questions.prompt: Why does the ERP show up in the average but hardly in a single trial?

options.text: Because the response repeats with the same shape and timing in every trial, while other activity is random and cancels out in the average
Because averaging removes high frequencies like a filter
Because averaging multiplies the signal by the number of trials
Because EEGLAB removes noisy trials before averaging

questions.explanation: A point-by-point average keeps what repeats with the same timing and weakens what varies at random from trial to trial. That is why the waveform gets clearer with more trials.

questions.prompt: You raise the number of trials in the average from 20 to 80, four times as many. Roughly what happens to the noise in the average?

options.text: It stays the same
It is halved
It drops to a quarter
It disappears completely

questions.explanation: Noise in the average falls with the square root of the number of trials, and the square root of 4 is 2, so it halves. That is why a small gain needs many trials, and why similar trial counts per condition matter.

questions.prompt: This is the D1 spectrum after removing ICA components, with a scalp map at 10 Hz. What do you read from it?

image.alt: Spectrum lines for all channels from 1 to 64 Hz, vertical axis 10*log10(µV²/Hz). A clear rise near 10 Hz, a gradual fall with frequency, and a narrow dip between 58 and 62 Hz. Above the spectrum, a scalp map at 10 Hz whose strongest colors are at the back of the head.
image.spec: The same image as the power-spectrum lesson (fig_power_spectrum.m on D1 main clean, 1 to 64 Hz, map at 10 Hz), unchanged. One version for both languages.

options.text: An alpha peak near 10 Hz, strongest at the back of the head
An alpha peak near 10 Hz, strongest at the front of the head
A line-noise peak at 60 Hz
The fall in power with frequency is a sign of a bad channel

questions.explanation: The rise near 10 Hz is the alpha peak, and the map shows it is strongest at posterior channels such as POz and Pz. At 60 Hz there is a dip, not a peak, left by the notch filter. The gradual fall with frequency (1/f) is the normal shape of every EEG signal.

questions.prompt: Which statements about reading a spectrum in EEGLAB are true? (Select all that apply)

options.text: A gradual fall in power as frequency rises is normal
A 10 dB difference means ten times more power
A narrow peak at 50 or 60 Hz in uncleaned data is a sign of line noise
The default plotting range of 2 to 25 Hz is enough to spot line noise
You compute the spectrum after a 30 Hz low-pass to see the full spectrum

questions.explanation: The vertical axis is logarithmic, so a difference in dB is a ratio, not units. The default range stops at 25 Hz, so 50 and 60 are not visible; widen it. After a 30 Hz low-pass everything above it is gone, so compute the spectrum before it.

questions.prompt: In an ERP plot from another program, the largest peak points down. Before you say it is negative, what do you check?

options.text: The direction of the vertical axis: is positive up or negative up
The number of channels in the dataset
The sampling rate
The line color

questions.explanation: Some books and programs plot negative up. In EEGLAB menus positive is up (the `'ydir', 1` option), but check the axis label of every plot before you say "positive peak" or "negative peak".
